extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of classical political philosophy; people studying Plato's Republic and theories of civic education
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and prescriptions for educating, testing, selecting, and provisioning the guardian (ruler/warrior) class in an ideal city — covering music and gymnastic training, diet, tests of character, qualifications for magistrates and physicians, communal living, and use of civic myth. Extracts standards embedded in Plato's discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical training as primary formative instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: “Musical training is a more potent instrument than any other, because rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul, on which they mightily fasten… imparting grace, and making the soul of him who is rightly educated graceful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music (rhythm and harmony) must be taught from earliest years because it imprints the soul; it enables one to perceive omissions or faults in art and nature and to form a true taste. Instruction should include recognising the essential forms of virtues (temperance, courage, liberality, magnificence) and their contraries in all combinations—analogous to learning letters so one can recognise them wherever they appear. Anti-pattern: neglecting musical training or treating it as frivolous.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of music: love of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus much of music, which makes a fair ending; for what should be the end of music if not the love of beauty?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music's telos is to inspire love of beauty and order; music that leads to intemperance, madness, or mere sensual pleasure is disallowed. Instruction should orient music toward temperate, harmonious love rather than sensual excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic training: simple, lifelong, and suited to warriors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gymnastic as well as music should begin in early years; the training in it should be careful and should continue through life... a finer sort of training will be required for our warrior athletes, who are to be like wakeful dogs, and to see and hear with the utmost keenness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical training should produce hardy, wakeful soldiers able to endure campaign hardships (changes of food, heat, cold) and not the 'sleepy sort' of athletes who become fragile when regimen changes. The preferred gymnastic is simple and military (e.g., Homeric soldier fare), avoiding over-refinement, elaborate sauces, or indulgent living that undermines robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must abstain from intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: “That they must abstain from intoxication has been already remarked by us; for of all persons a guardian should be the last to get drunk and not know where in the world he is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must be sober and self-governing; being incapacitated by drink is intolerable and undermines their role. Anti-pattern: requiring another guardian to take care of a drunk guardian is ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of diet and regimen to safeguard health and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “Simplicity in music was the parent of temperance in the soul; and simplicity in gymnastic of health in the body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid complex, luxurious food and lifestyle (sweet sauces, refined cookery, decadent companionship) because complexity engenders disease and moral licence; simplicity produces temperance in soul and health in body. Over-refinement leads to proliferation of doctors and lawyers and to a disgraceful state of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicine should treat definite acute ailments and not cultivate hypochondria
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors should cure those with definite ailments and not lengthen out 'good-for-nothing lives' by treating valetudinarian conditions; the medical art must serve the State's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicians should not indulge or invent chronic conditions that distract citizens from their occupations; medicine that 'educates diseases' (Herodicus' lingering-death approach) is condemned. Treatment is appropriate for those with definite employments who need temporary cures, not for prolonging useless lives. This standard ties medical practice to civic utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician qualifications: broad experience of disease
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most skilful physicians are those who, from their youth upwards, have combined with the knowledge of their art the greatest experience of disease; they had better not be robust in health, and should have had all manner of diseases in their own persons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good physicians should have extensive firsthand experience of varied illnesses—so the mind that has been sick can recognize and treat disease. This is appropriate because physicians cure ‘with the mind’ rather than via the body as instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge qualifications: moral purity and observational knowledge of evil
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the judge it is otherwise; since he governs mind by mind; he ought not therefore to have been trained among vicious minds... The honourable mind which is to form a healthy judgment should have had no experience or contamination of evil habits when young.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should be morally uncontaminated in youth and gain knowledge of vice only through later observation of others; they should be older and guided by knowledge, not by personal experience of wrongdoing. Anti-pattern: a judge who has practised many crimes—he may be suspicious, crafty, and unfit to recognise actual virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance/harmony of musical and gymnastic education
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are two principles of human nature, one the spirited and the other the philosophical... one who mingles music with gymnastic in the fairest proportions... may be rightly called the true musician and harmonist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive devotion to gymnastic produces hardness and ferocity; exclusive devotion to music produces softness and effeminacy. Proper education harmonizes spirit (courage) and reason (gentleness) through balanced music and gymnastic so guardians are both temperate and courageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of soul as standard of character (temperance + courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: “And the harmonious soul is both temperate and courageous; and the inharmonious is cowardly and boorish.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-ordered soul exhibits both temperance and courage. Educational aims and selection procedures should produce and detect this harmony. Anti-patterns: souls that are excessively soft (wasted spirit) or excessively hard (brutal ferocity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and continuous testing of guardians throughout life
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must watch them from their youth upwards... make them perform actions in which they are most likely to forget or to be deceived, and he who remembers and is not deceived is to be selected... And there should also be toils and pains and conflicts prescribed for them... And then, I said, we must try them with enchantments—that is the third sort of test—and see what will be their behaviour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is ongoing: monitor candidates at every age, subject them to trials of toil, pain, fear, pleasure (enchantments), and tests of argument (theft), force, and enchantment. Choose those who retain conviction and are not deceived or corrupted; reject failures. Tests are meant to reveal whether they are 'armed against all enchantments' and consistently rhythmic and harmonious in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disposition for guardians: love of the city and its good
rubrics_metrics.description: “They who in their whole life show the greatest eagerness to do what is for the good of their country, and the greatest repugnance to do what is against her interests... Those are the right men.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians should be selected for demonstrable love and care for the city—i.e., they must identify their interests with the city's and be disposed to protect it. This quality is a primary selection criterion alongside performance in trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of rulers vs auxiliaries and role-based character
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps the word ‘guardian’ in the fullest sense ought to be applied to this higher class only... The young men we before called guardians may be more properly designated auxiliaries and supporters of the principles of the rulers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best of the guardian class become rulers; others serve as auxiliaries. Roles should match character and training: rulers require the highest proof of virtue and temperamental fitness; auxiliaries support and enforce the rulers' principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal living and property restrictions on guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: “None of them should have any property of his own beyond what is absolutely necessary; neither should they have a private house or store closed against any one... they should agree to receive from the citizens a fixed rate of pay... they will go to mess and live together like soldiers... And they alone of all the citizens may not touch or handle silver or gold.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent guardians becoming housekeepers, husbandmen, enemies, or tyrants, they must have minimal private property, communal mess-halls, fixed pay, no private houses, and an absolute prohibition on touching money (gold/silver). These institutional arrangements are designed to eliminate private incentives that corrupt guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dwellings and accoutrements must prevent predatory behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their dwellings must be such as will neither impair their virtue as guardians, nor tempt them to prey upon the other citizens... the houses of soldiers, and not of shop-keepers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housing, furnishings, and all material conditions should be arranged to avoid impairing virtue or creating temptations to exploit other citizens. Practical design of auxiliary/ruler accommodations is part of civic policy to deter internal depredation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a civic 'noble lie' to promote unity and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are to be told that their youth was a dream... in reality during all that time they were being formed and fed in the womb of the earth... Citizens... you are brothers, yet God has framed you differently... some... mingled gold... others silver... others brass and iron... the rulers... must anxiously guard... the purity of the race.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sanctioned myth (the 'royal lie') is to be taught to rulers, soldiers, and people to foster attachment to the city and acceptance of social roles. The tale includes earth-born origin and metals-in-soul allegory, and a doctrine that rulers must guard the 'purity' of the race while allowing occasional transposition of ranks. Plato acknowledges practical difficulties in persuading current generations but recommends inculcation across posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and punishment for selection outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who at every age... has come out of the trial victorious and pure, shall be appointed a ruler... he shall be honoured in life and death... But him who fails, we must reject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful candidates receive civic honours, burial memorials, and office; unsuccessful ones are excluded. This establishes clear incentives and social recognition tied to the selection and testing regimen.
